newsitem.title: USA: Clinton meets senators on chemical weapons treaty.
newsitem.headline: Clinton meets senators on chemical weapons treaty.

text.p: President Bill Clinton met eight senators at the White House on Wednesday in an effort to to win Senate ratification of the Chemical Weapons Convention.

The White House is pushing the Senate to vote soon on the treaty, which bans the development, production, stockpiling, transfer and use of chemical weapons, in order to meet an April 29 deadline, when the agreement comes into force.

"This was an opportunity for the president to continue to make a very strong case for ratification ... because it is in the best interests of the security of the United States and of our troops," a White House spokesman said after the meeting attended by Secretary of State Madeleine Albright.

As they left the White House, several senators said the treaty would win ratification if it makes it to a full Senate vote, but were more guarded on the matter of whether it would escape the Senate Foreign Relations Committee for such a vote.
"I think we have enough votes to ratify the treaty," said Sen. Joe Biden, a Delaware Democrat. "The only question is how we get the treaty up (for a vote)."
He added: "I take it on faith that we will get a chance to get the treaty up and get it voted on -- if we have a chance to vote, I'm convinced we have the votes to pass the treaty."

Biden has been negotiating with the Republican chairman of the committee, Sen. Jesse Helms of North Carolina, to iron out their differences on the document, which was negotiated under former Republican President George Bush and signed in 1993.

"My hope is that when all (is) said and done, the treaty will be passed," said Sen. Arlen Specter, a Pennsylvania Republican, as he left the meeting. "I think that we are going to see some indicators that some of the objections which have been raised by a number of senators will be met."

One U.S. official said the Senate would have to vote next week to meet the April 29 deadline because of the April 21-22 Jewish holiday of Passover and the formalities of submitting the ratified document to the United Nations in New York.
The treaty requires a two-thirds majority to pass in the 100-member Senate.
